tooltip.title: Treatment of Chronic Kidney Disease-Associated Pruritus
tooltip.markdown: Management involves optimizing dialysis, aggressive skincare, and targeting the neuropathic/opioidergic components of the itch.

tooltip.title: Optimize Dialysis
tooltip.markdown: Ensure adequacy of hemodialysis as a first step.

tooltip.title: Aggressive Emollient Use
tooltip.markdown: Essential for managing the xerosis that is almost always present and contributes to itch.

tooltip.title: Gabapentinoids
tooltip.markdown: Gabapentinoids can be considered off-label with cautious renal/dialysis-adjusted dosing and monitoring for sedation, confusion and falls. Do not apply a general-population dose or an automatic oral first-line requirement to every dialysis patient.

tooltip.title: Second-Line Therapies
tooltip.markdown: For patients who do not respond to first-line agents.

tooltip.title: Phototherapy
tooltip.markdown: Broadband or narrowband UVB is an effective option.

tooltip.title: Naltrexone
tooltip.markdown: The μ-opioid antagonist can be effective, though results in trials have been mixed.

tooltip.title: Third-Line and Emerging Therapies
tooltip.markdown: Treatment choices depend on dialysis modality, symptom severity, response, availability and safety; this section is not a validated mandatory third-line sequence.

tooltip.title: Mirtazapine
tooltip.markdown: A low-dose antidepressant that can be helpful, particularly for nocturnal itch due to its sedative effects.

tooltip.title: Difelikefalin
tooltip.markdown: Difelikefalin is an approved option for moderate-to-severe CKD-associated pruritus in adults undergoing hemodialysis. That indication must not be generalized to nondialysis CKD or peritoneal dialysis. Assess CNS adverse effects and use the current product-specific administration instructions.
